items.title: I can differentiate between open and closed systems
items.what: An open system allows both energy and matter to transfer between the reaction and its surroundings. A closed system allows energy transfer but not matter.
items.why: The type of system determines which measurement methods are valid and how the reaction behaves over time.
items.example: A flask with a loose top is an open system — gas can escape. A flask with a tightly sealed stopper is a closed system — gases produced are trapped inside.

subtopic.name: Systems and Monitoring Reaction Rate
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the difference between open and closed systems and how the system type affects a reaction. It also explores different methods for measuring the rate of a chemical reaction over time.
subtopic.why: Understanding systems is essential for interpreting experimental data and designing investigations. Knowing how to measure reaction rate underpins all experimental work in kinetics.

items.title: I can outline how reactions proceed differently in open and closed systems
items.what: In an open system, gaseous products escape to the surroundings and cannot re-react. In a closed system, all reactants and products remain within the reaction vessel.
items.why: The system type affects whether concentration of products builds up, which in turn influences the rate and extent of the reaction.
items.example: Magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid in an open flask releases hydrogen gas into the air. In a sealed flask, the hydrogen gas accumulates inside the vessel.

subtopic.name: Systems and Monitoring Reaction Rate
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the difference between open and closed systems and how the system type affects a reaction. It also explores different methods for measuring the rate of a chemical reaction over time.
subtopic.why: Understanding systems is essential for interpreting experimental data and designing investigations. Knowing how to measure reaction rate underpins all experimental work in kinetics.

items.title: I can describe how the rate of a reaction can be monitored by measuring changes in concentration over time
items.what: Reaction rate can be measured by tracking how the concentration of a reactant decreases or how the concentration of a product increases over time.
items.why: Measuring concentration over time gives a direct indication of how fast reactants are being consumed and products are being formed.
items.example: In the reaction of sodium ions with phosphate ions, measuring the decrease in sodium ion concentration (mol/L) at regular time intervals allows the rate to be calculated.

subtopic.name: Systems and Monitoring Reaction Rate
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the difference between open and closed systems and how the system type affects a reaction. It also explores different methods for measuring the rate of a chemical reaction over time.
subtopic.why: Understanding systems is essential for interpreting experimental data and designing investigations. Knowing how to measure reaction rate underpins all experimental work in kinetics.

items.title: I can describe how the rate of a reaction can be monitored by measuring changes in gas volume or mass over time
items.what: If a reaction produces a gas, the volume of gas collected can be measured over time. In an open system, the loss of mass as gas escapes can also be measured.
items.why: Concentration is not always practical to measure directly. Volume and mass are often easier to record with standard lab equipment.
items.example: In the reaction of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid, carbon dioxide gas is produced. Placing the flask on a balance and recording the decrease in mass every 60 seconds gives a measure of reaction rate.

subtopic.name: Systems and Monitoring Reaction Rate
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the difference between open and closed systems and how the system type affects a reaction. It also explores different methods for measuring the rate of a chemical reaction over time.
subtopic.why: Understanding systems is essential for interpreting experimental data and designing investigations. Knowing how to measure reaction rate underpins all experimental work in kinetics.

items.title: I can express reaction rate mathematically using change in concentration divided by change in time
items.what: Reaction rate is calculated as the change in concentration (Δc) divided by the change in time (Δt). Similar expressions apply when using mass or volume instead of concentration.
items.why: A mathematical definition allows rates to be compared quantitatively between different experiments and conditions.
items.example: If the concentration of a reactant drops from 0.80 mol/L to 0.50 mol/L over 30 seconds, the rate is (0.80 - 0.50) / 30 = 0.01 mol/L/s.

subtopic.why: Understanding systems is essential for interpreting experimental data and designing investigations. Knowing how to measure reaction rate underpins all experimental work in kinetics.

items.title: I can describe the three conditions that must be met for a successful collision
items.what: For a reaction to occur, particles must (1) collide with each other, (2) collide with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, and (3) collide in the correct orientation.
items.why: These three conditions explain why reactions do not occur simply because reactants are present — the quality and alignment of collisions matter.
items.example: Hydrogen molecules colliding with oxygen molecules will only produce water if they collide with enough kinetic energy to overcome the activation energy and are aligned so bonding can occur.

subtopic.name: Collision Theory
subtopic.what: Collision theory describes the three conditions that must be met for a chemical reaction to occur: particles must collide, with sufficient energy, and in the correct orientation. It explains why not every collision results in a reaction.
subtopic.why: Collision theory is the conceptual foundation for understanding all factors that affect reaction rate. Every explanation of why temperature, concentration or catalysts change the rate links back to these three conditions.

items.title: I can explain what activation energy is and how it relates to collision theory
items.what: Activation energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles must possess for a reaction to occur. It represents an energy barrier that reactants must overcome to form products.
items.why: Activation energy explains why some reactions are fast and others are slow at the same temperature — lower activation energy means more particles can react.
items.example: On an energy profile diagram for an exothermic reaction, the activation energy is shown as the energy difference between the reactants and the peak of the curve (the transition state).

subtopic.name: Collision Theory
subtopic.what: Collision theory describes the three conditions that must be met for a chemical reaction to occur: particles must collide, with sufficient energy, and in the correct orientation. It explains why not every collision results in a reaction.
subtopic.why: Collision theory is the conceptual foundation for understanding all factors that affect reaction rate. Every explanation of why temperature, concentration or catalysts change the rate links back to these three conditions.

items.title: I can explain how orientation affects whether a collision is successful
items.what: Even if two particles collide with sufficient energy, the reaction will not occur if the particles are not aligned in the correct geometry for bonds to break and form.
items.why: Orientation explains why reactions can have a low success rate even when particles have enough energy — a poor geometric alignment prevents product formation.
items.example: If two XY molecules collide end-to-end in the correct alignment, the X-X and Y-Y bonds can form. If they collide side-on in the wrong alignment, the molecules simply bounce apart and no reaction occurs.

subtopic.name: Collision Theory
subtopic.what: Collision theory describes the three conditions that must be met for a chemical reaction to occur: particles must collide, with sufficient energy, and in the correct orientation. It explains why not every collision results in a reaction.
subtopic.why: Collision theory is the conceptual foundation for understanding all factors that affect reaction rate. Every explanation of why temperature, concentration or catalysts change the rate links back to these three conditions.

items.title: I can identify the four possible outcomes of a particle collision
items.what: The four outcomes are: incorrect orientation and insufficient energy (no reaction); incorrect orientation and sufficient energy (no reaction); correct orientation and insufficient energy (no reaction); correct orientation and sufficient energy (reaction occurs).
items.why: Understanding that only one of four possible collision outcomes leads to a reaction helps explain why reaction rates are often low even in concentrated mixtures.
items.example: Two gas particles with high kinetic energy collide, but one approaches from the wrong angle — despite having more than enough energy, no reaction takes place because the orientation is incorrect.

subtopic.name: Collision Theory
subtopic.what: Collision theory describes the three conditions that must be met for a chemical reaction to occur: particles must collide, with sufficient energy, and in the correct orientation. It explains why not every collision results in a reaction.
subtopic.why: Collision theory is the conceptual foundation for understanding all factors that affect reaction rate. Every explanation of why temperature, concentration or catalysts change the rate links back to these three conditions.

items.title: I can draw and label an energy profile diagram showing activation energy for exothermic and endothermic reactions
items.what: An energy profile diagram plots energy against the progress of reaction. The activation energy is the difference between the reactants' energy level and the peak of the curve.
items.why: Energy profile diagrams provide a visual way to compare the energy requirements of different reactions and to illustrate the effect of catalysts.
items.example: For an exothermic reaction, the products sit lower on the energy axis than the reactants. The activation energy arrow points from the reactants' energy level up to the peak of the curve.

subtopic.name: Collision Theory
subtopic.what: Collision theory describes the three conditions that must be met for a chemical reaction to occur: particles must collide, with sufficient energy, and in the correct orientation. It explains why not every collision results in a reaction.
subtopic.why: Collision theory is the conceptual foundation for understanding all factors that affect reaction rate. Every explanation of why temperature, concentration or catalysts change the rate links back to these three conditions.

items.title: I can explain the relationship between concentration and rate of reaction using collision theory
items.what: Increasing the concentration of a solution increases the number of particles in a given volume. This increases the frequency of collisions between reactant particles, leading to a higher rate of reaction.
items.why: Collision frequency is a key driver of reaction rate. More collisions per unit time means more opportunities for successful reactions to occur.
items.example: A 1.0 mol/L solution of hydrochloric acid reacts faster with calcium carbonate than a 0.1 mol/L solution because there are ten times more H+ ions in the same volume, increasing collision frequency.

subtopic.name: Concentration and Gas Pressure
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how increasing the concentration of a solution or the pressure of a gas increases the rate of reaction. Both factors act by increasing the frequency of particle collisions.
subtopic.why: Concentration and pressure are among the most commonly adjusted variables in industrial chemistry. Understanding their effect on rate allows chemists to control and optimise reactions.

items.title: I can identify which aspects of collision theory are affected by a change in concentration
items.what: Increasing concentration increases collision frequency. It does not affect the energy of individual collisions or the orientation of collisions.
items.why: Being precise about which part of collision theory is affected allows for accurate and complete exam answers.
items.example: Doubling the concentration of sodium hydroxide in a reaction doubles the likelihood of particles meeting, but the kinetic energy of each particle and the geometry of each collision remain unchanged.

subtopic.name: Concentration and Gas Pressure
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how increasing the concentration of a solution or the pressure of a gas increases the rate of reaction. Both factors act by increasing the frequency of particle collisions.
subtopic.why: Concentration and pressure are among the most commonly adjusted variables in industrial chemistry. Understanding their effect on rate allows chemists to control and optimise reactions.

items.title: I can explain the relationship between gas pressure and rate of reaction using collision theory
items.what: Increasing gas pressure by decreasing the volume of the reaction vessel forces the same number of gas particles into a smaller space. This increases collision frequency and therefore the rate of reaction.
items.why: Gas pressure is the equivalent of concentration for gaseous reactions. Controlling vessel volume is a practical way to control reaction rate in industrial gas-phase reactions.
items.example: The same number of gas particles in a 100 mL container will collide more frequently than in a 1 L container, because they are more densely packed and encounter each other more often.

subtopic.name: Concentration and Gas Pressure
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how increasing the concentration of a solution or the pressure of a gas increases the rate of reaction. Both factors act by increasing the frequency of particle collisions.
subtopic.why: Concentration and pressure are among the most commonly adjusted variables in industrial chemistry. Understanding their effect on rate allows chemists to control and optimise reactions.

items.title: I can identify which aspects of collision theory are affected by a change in gas pressure
items.what: Increasing gas pressure increases collision frequency. It does not affect the energy of individual particles or the orientation of their collisions.
items.why: Understanding the specific mechanism avoids the common error of assuming that pressure changes the energy of particles.
items.example: Compressing a gas reaction from 250 mL to 100 mL increases how often particles collide, but each individual particle still has the same kinetic energy as before the compression.

subtopic.name: Concentration and Gas Pressure
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how increasing the concentration of a solution or the pressure of a gas increases the rate of reaction. Both factors act by increasing the frequency of particle collisions.
subtopic.why: Concentration and pressure are among the most commonly adjusted variables in industrial chemistry. Understanding their effect on rate allows chemists to control and optimise reactions.

items.title: I can explain the relationship between surface area and rate of reaction using collision theory
items.what: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant exposes more particles to the other reactant, increasing the frequency of collisions. Only particles on the exposed surface can participate in collisions.
items.why: Many reactions involve a solid and a liquid or gas. Grinding the solid into smaller pieces dramatically increases the available surface for reaction.
items.example: Powdered calcium carbonate reacts much faster with hydrochloric acid than a large block of the same mass, because far more CaCO3 particles are exposed and available to collide with H+ ions.

subtopic.name: Surface Area and Temperature
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how increasing surface area and increasing temperature both increase the rate of reaction, but through different mechanisms. Surface area affects collision frequency, while temperature affects both collision frequency and collision energy.
subtopic.why: Temperature is the most significant variable affecting reaction rate in most real-world and industrial contexts. Surface area is particularly important in heterogeneous reactions involving solids.

items.title: I can identify which aspects of collision theory are affected by a change in surface area
items.what: Increasing surface area increases collision frequency only. It does not affect the energy of collisions or the orientation of collisions.
items.why: Surface area only determines how many particles are accessible — it does not change how energetically or how well-aligned those collisions are.
items.example: Breaking a block of magnesium into small chips does not give any individual magnesium atom more kinetic energy — it simply makes more atoms available to collide with acid molecules.

subtopic.name: Surface Area and Temperature
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how increasing surface area and increasing temperature both increase the rate of reaction, but through different mechanisms. Surface area affects collision frequency, while temperature affects both collision frequency and collision energy.
subtopic.why: Temperature is the most significant variable affecting reaction rate in most real-world and industrial contexts. Surface area is particularly important in heterogeneous reactions involving solids.

items.title: I can explain the relationship between temperature and rate of reaction using collision theory
items.what: Increasing temperature increases the kinetic energy of particles. This increases both the frequency of collisions and the proportion of collisions that have energy greater than the activation energy, leading to a higher rate of reaction.
items.why: Temperature is unique among the rate factors because it affects two aspects of collision theory simultaneously, making it a particularly powerful way to change reaction rate.
items.example: Heating hydrochloric acid from 20°C to 40°C before adding calcium carbonate causes the reaction to proceed noticeably faster, because more acid particles are moving quickly enough to exceed the activation energy on collision.

subtopic.name: Surface Area and Temperature
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how increasing surface area and increasing temperature both increase the rate of reaction, but through different mechanisms. Surface area affects collision frequency, while temperature affects both collision frequency and collision energy.
subtopic.why: Temperature is the most significant variable affecting reaction rate in most real-world and industrial contexts. Surface area is particularly important in heterogeneous reactions involving solids.

items.title: I can identify which aspects of collision theory are affected by a change in temperature
items.what: Increasing temperature increases collision frequency and increases the proportion of collisions with sufficient energy to react. It does not affect the orientation of collisions.
items.why: Temperature is the only common factor (other than catalysts) that increases the proportion of energetically successful collisions, not just the total number of collisions.
items.example: At 30°C compared to 10°C, particles in a reaction mixture move faster (more collisions per second) and more of those collisions exceed the activation energy, both contributing to the faster rate.

subtopic.name: Surface Area and Temperature
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how increasing surface area and increasing temperature both increase the rate of reaction, but through different mechanisms. Surface area affects collision frequency, while temperature affects both collision frequency and collision energy.
subtopic.why: Temperature is the most significant variable affecting reaction rate in most real-world and industrial contexts. Surface area is particularly important in heterogeneous reactions involving solids.

items.title: I can outline the effect of temperature on reaction rate using a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve
items.what: A Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve shows the spread of kinetic energies among particles at a given temperature. At higher temperatures, the curve flattens and shifts to the right, meaning more particles have high energies.
items.why: The Maxwell-Boltzmann curve provides a visual and quantitative way to explain why temperature has such a strong effect on reaction rate.
items.example: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve comparing T1 (lower) and T2 (higher), the area under the curve to the right of the activation energy line is larger at T2, showing that more particles can react at the higher temperature.

subtopic.name: Surface Area and Temperature
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how increasing surface area and increasing temperature both increase the rate of reaction, but through different mechanisms. Surface area affects collision frequency, while temperature affects both collision frequency and collision energy.
subtopic.why: Temperature is the most significant variable affecting reaction rate in most real-world and industrial contexts. Surface area is particularly important in heterogeneous reactions involving solids.

items.title: I can explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction
items.what: A catalyst increases reaction rate by providing an alternative reaction pathway that has a lower activation energy. More particles can now collide with sufficient energy to react, so the reaction proceeds faster.
items.why: Understanding the mechanism of catalysis is important for interpreting energy diagrams and for applying this knowledge to biological enzymes in later topics.
items.example: In a catalytic converter, platinum metal provides a surface on which exhaust gases can react at a much lower activation energy than they would require in the gas phase, speeding up their conversion to less harmful products.

subtopic.name: Catalysts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how catalysts increase reaction rate by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. It also distinguishes between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts.
subtopic.why: Catalysts are essential in industrial chemistry and biology. Many large-scale manufacturing processes and virtually all biochemical reactions depend on catalysts to proceed at useful rates.

items.title: I can state that a catalyst is not consumed during a reaction
items.what: A catalyst participates in the reaction mechanism but is regenerated by the end of the reaction. It is not used up and remains available to catalyse further reactions.
items.why: This property makes catalysts economically valuable — a small amount can facilitate a very large number of reactions without being depleted.
items.example: The enzyme amylase in saliva catalyses the breakdown of starch into sugars. The amylase molecules are not consumed in the process and can continue to act on more starch molecules.

subtopic.name: Catalysts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how catalysts increase reaction rate by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. It also distinguishes between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts.
subtopic.why: Catalysts are essential in industrial chemistry and biology. Many large-scale manufacturing processes and virtually all biochemical reactions depend on catalysts to proceed at useful rates.

items.title: I can outline the effect of a catalyst on rate of reaction using an energy profile diagram
items.what: On an energy profile diagram, a catalyst is shown as an alternative pathway with a lower peak (lower activation energy) compared to the uncatalysed pathway. The energy levels of the reactants and products remain the same.
items.why: Energy profile diagrams make it visually clear that a catalyst lowers the energy barrier, not the overall energy change of the reaction.
items.example: For an endothermic reaction, the catalysed pathway shows a lower hump between reactants and products. The reactants and products sit at the same energy levels as the uncatalysed version, but the peak in between is lower.

subtopic.name: Catalysts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how catalysts increase reaction rate by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. It also distinguishes between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts.
subtopic.why: Catalysts are essential in industrial chemistry and biology. Many large-scale manufacturing processes and virtually all biochemical reactions depend on catalysts to proceed at useful rates.

items.title: I can distinguish between the mechanism of a catalyst and that of a temperature increase
items.what: A temperature increase gives particles more kinetic energy so that more of them exceed the (unchanged) activation energy. A catalyst lowers the activation energy threshold itself, so that more particles can exceed it without gaining extra energy.
items.why: This distinction is frequently tested and is important for understanding why these two strategies have different practical applications.
items.example: Lowering the pass mark for an exam from 80% to 60% (catalyst analogy) allows more students to pass without studying more. Running extra tutorials so more students score above 80% (temperature analogy) raises their performance instead.

subtopic.name: Catalysts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how catalysts increase reaction rate by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. It also distinguishes between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts.
subtopic.why: Catalysts are essential in industrial chemistry and biology. Many large-scale manufacturing processes and virtually all biochemical reactions depend on catalysts to proceed at useful rates.

items.title: I can distinguish between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts
items.what: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same physical state or phase as the reactants. A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different physical state or phase from the reactants.
items.why: The distinction between catalyst types is relevant to how catalysts are used industrially and biologically, and to understanding how catalyst surface area affects efficiency.
items.example: A solid platinum catalyst in a catalytic converter is heterogeneous — the reactants are gases and the catalyst is a solid. An aqueous enzyme catalysing a reaction in solution is homogeneous — both are in the aqueous phase.

subtopic.name: Catalysts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how catalysts increase reaction rate by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. It also distinguishes between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts.
subtopic.why: Catalysts are essential in industrial chemistry and biology. Many large-scale manufacturing processes and virtually all biochemical reactions depend on catalysts to proceed at useful rates.

items.title: I can describe the key features of a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve
items.what: The x-axis shows kinetic energy and the y-axis shows the proportion of molecules with that energy. The curve starts at zero, rises to a peak, then tails off to the right. The area under the curve represents the total number of particles.
items.why: A correct understanding of the curve's shape and axes is necessary before it can be used to explain temperature and catalyst effects.
items.example: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, most particles cluster around the peak energy, while only a small proportion of particles have very low or very high energies. The curve never touches the x-axis on the right because some particles always have very high energy.

subtopic.name: Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
subtopic.what: This subtopic focuses on using Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves to explain and illustrate the effects of temperature and catalysts on reaction rate. The curve shows how kinetic energy is distributed among particles in a sample.
subtopic.why: Maxwell-Boltzmann curves are a key analytical and exam tool. They allow quantitative and visual reasoning about why rate changes occur, and they appear regularly in VCE exam questions.

items.title: I can use a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve to explain the effect of increasing temperature on reaction rate
items.what: At a higher temperature, the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve flattens and shifts to the right. The area under the curve to the right of the activation energy line is larger, meaning more particles have sufficient energy to react.
items.why: This provides a graphical explanation for why reaction rate increases with temperature that goes beyond a simple statement of the relationship.
items.example: On a diagram showing curves for T1 and T2 (where T2 is higher), the shaded area to the right of the Ea line is visibly larger for T2. This shows that at T2 a greater proportion of particles will have successful collisions.

subtopic.name: Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
subtopic.what: This subtopic focuses on using Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves to explain and illustrate the effects of temperature and catalysts on reaction rate. The curve shows how kinetic energy is distributed among particles in a sample.
subtopic.why: Maxwell-Boltzmann curves are a key analytical and exam tool. They allow quantitative and visual reasoning about why rate changes occur, and they appear regularly in VCE exam questions.

items.title: I can describe the shape differences between a low-temperature and high-temperature Maxwell-Boltzmann curve
items.what: A lower temperature curve is taller and narrower, with its peak shifted to the left. A higher temperature curve is shorter and broader, with its peak shifted to the right. The total area under both curves remains the same.
items.why: Correctly drawing the shape difference between two temperature curves is a common exam requirement and demonstrates understanding beyond memorisation.
items.example: A Maxwell-Boltzmann curve for a reaction at 4°C will have a higher, narrower peak positioned further left compared to the curve at 25°C, which is lower, broader, and shifted to the right.

subtopic.name: Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
subtopic.what: This subtopic focuses on using Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves to explain and illustrate the effects of temperature and catalysts on reaction rate. The curve shows how kinetic energy is distributed among particles in a sample.
subtopic.why: Maxwell-Boltzmann curves are a key analytical and exam tool. They allow quantitative and visual reasoning about why rate changes occur, and they appear regularly in VCE exam questions.

items.title: I can use a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve to explain the effect of a catalyst on reaction rate
items.what: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the Ea line on the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve shifts to the left. The particle distribution itself does not change. A larger area under the curve now lies to the right of the (lower) Ea line.
items.why: This graphical approach makes it clear that a catalyst works by lowering the threshold, not by changing the energy of particles — a distinction that is frequently assessed.
items.example: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, adding a catalyst moves the Ea marker from 50 kJ/mol to 30 kJ/mol to the left. The curve stays the same shape, but the shaded area representing particles that can react is now much larger.

subtopic.name: Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
subtopic.what: This subtopic focuses on using Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves to explain and illustrate the effects of temperature and catalysts on reaction rate. The curve shows how kinetic energy is distributed among particles in a sample.
subtopic.why: Maxwell-Boltzmann curves are a key analytical and exam tool. They allow quantitative and visual reasoning about why rate changes occur, and they appear regularly in VCE exam questions.

items.title: I can compare the Maxwell-Boltzmann representations of a temperature increase and a catalyst on the same diagram
items.what: A temperature increase shifts the distribution curve to the right while leaving the Ea marker fixed. A catalyst shifts the Ea marker to the left while leaving the distribution curve unchanged. Both result in a larger proportion of particles being able to react.
items.why: Being able to distinguish between these two representations on a single diagram demonstrates a thorough understanding of both mechanisms.
items.example: On a diagram with a single Maxwell-Boltzmann curve and two Ea markers — one for uncatalysed and one for catalysed reactions — the shaded area between the two Ea markers represents the additional particles that can react only when the catalyst is present.
